newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservative Clarke hits out at rival Hague.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservative Clarke hits out at rival Hague.

text.p: The battle to lead Britain's defeated Conservative party plumbed new depths of acrimony on Tuesday as former finance minister Kenneth Clarke attacked his main rival William Hague for being a divisive opportunist.
Hague's insistence that any Conservatives who wanted to serve in his shadow cabinet would have to declare their opposition to a single currency was a recipe for division, Clarke told BBC radio.

"That is not the campaign of a unity candidate. That is the campaign of a candidate who's trying to settle an old issue," Clarke said shortly before the party's 164 MPs started to vote in the second ballot for a leader to succeed John Major.
Clarke, who topped last Tuesday's first ballot, said he was confident of winning, but Hague is the clear favourite. Right-wing Euro-sceptic John Redwood is expected to come last.
If, as expected, there is no outright winner when the result of the vote is announced around 1620 GMT, the two front-runners will square off on Thursday.

Clarke said he was the candidate who had the political skill and experience to unite the party -- although he admitted it would be hard to achieve -- and provide effective opposition to Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair.
But he expressed frustration that the leadership campaign had become yet again a referendum on the party's stance on Europe.

"Unfortunately in the second round of voting I fear there's a section of the party that's gone back to losing interest in the big subject and deciding to refight some of the battles before the last election and define now precise attitudes on the European single currency," Clarke said.
He accused Hague of changing his position several times before finally demanding that would-be shadow ministers back his line that a Conservative government would not scrap the pound.

This was a peculiar way to form a shadow cabinet, Clarke said. "What he's defined during the campaign is what he says is a very clear view on the single currency, which is quite different from the one he held a month ago.
"And apparently it's to be the one shibboleth you must pronounce as you enter the camp and that is to be predetermined before anybody sits down," Clarke said.
Redwood also accused Hague of changing his mind on the single currency. "Clarity is what we need," he told BBC radio.

He hoped Clarke would serve under his leadership but said the former chancellor of the exchequer would be expected to toe his line. Unlike Clarke, who has an open mind on the single currency, Redwood is fundamentally opposed to it.
